scenario: You need to record a full capacity assessment for a newly admitted patient.
question: In SystmOne, which route does the trust Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) tell you to take to start a full Mental Capacity Act (MCA) capacity assessment?
options: Select the patient, click Launch Pad, then click the MCA Capacity/Competency tab
Select the patient, click Alerts at the bottom of the page, then Patient Alert Indicators
Open the care plan and add a Capacity section as free text
Open the patient's Risk screen and select Capacity from the domain list
rationale: The Capacity and Competency SOP sets out the process as: select patient, click Launch Pad, click the MCA Capacity/Competency tab, then Capacity to consent (MCA). The Alerts route is the one used for advance statements and Power of Attorney, not capacity assessments.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Standard Operating Procedure: Capacity and Competency
sourceDate: Issue 1, trust wide, no issue or review date printed on the document

question: A patient's presentation and care plan are both unchanged, but time has passed since their last recorded formal capacity assessment. Under the trust Standard Operating Procedure (SOP), after how long should a further full capacity assessment always be completed?
options: 3 months
6 months
12 months
2 years
rationale: The Capacity and Competency SOP lists three triggers for a further full assessment: a significant change in presentation, a change in the care plan with a new and significant intervention, or 12 months since a formal capacity assessment was recorded.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Standard Operating Procedure: Capacity and Competency
sourceDate: Issue 1, trust wide, no issue or review date printed on the document

scenario: After seeing a patient you make a case entry and notice the Capacity/Competency drop-down box.
question: Under the trust Standard Operating Procedure (SOP), when may you record capacity using that drop-down box rather than completing a full assessment?
options: Any time the decision is a day to day one
Only if a full capacity assessment has already been completed and it is allied to the current care plan
Only if a doctor has countersigned the entry
Only during the first 72 hours of admission
rationale: The SOP is explicit that the drop-down facility can only be used if a full capacity assessment has already been completed which is allied to the current care plan.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Standard Operating Procedure: Capacity and Competency
sourceDate: Issue 1, trust wide, no issue or review date printed on the document

scenario: A capacity assessment on SystmOne concludes that the patient lacks capacity for the decision in question.
question: Which SystmOne tab does the trust Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) say you complete next?
options: The Consent to Share tab
The Mental Health Act (MHA) Legal Status tab
The DHCFT Best Interest Decision tab
The Safeguarding Referral tab
rationale: The SOP states that if the patient lacks capacity you click the DHCFT Best Interest Decision tab and complete the Best Interest questionnaire, saving either for future editing or as a final version.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Standard Operating Procedure: Capacity and Competency
sourceDate: Issue 1, trust wide, no issue or review date printed on the document

scenario: A patient has told you they have made an advance statement and named a relative with Power of Attorney.
question: Under the trust Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for Advanced Statements, Power of Attorney (POA) and Do Not Attempt Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (DNACPR), how is this flagged on SystmOne?
options: It is typed into the daily progress note only
It is added to the handover sheet by the nurse in charge
It is emailed to the Mental Health Act (MHA) office to add centrally
It is entered via Alerts from the ward view, and a red exclamation mark then appears on the patient details box
rationale: The SOP process is: from ward view select the patient, click Alerts, complete the Patient Alert Indicators box and save. The alert then shows on the bed view and a red exclamation mark appears on the patient details box, which you hover over to see the recorded alerts.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Standard Operating Procedure: Advanced Statements, POA/DNACPR
sourceDate: Issue 1, trust wide, no issue or review date printed on the document

question: Under the trust Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) policy, an urgent authorisation that the Trust grants itself makes the deprivation of liberty lawful for a period not exceeding how long?
options: 24 hours
72 hours
7 days
14 days
rationale: The DoLS policy states the Managing Authority may grant itself an urgent authorisation lasting no more than 7 days, and that a request for standard authorisation must be made at the same time.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Deprivation of Liberty (DoLS) Policy and Procedures
sourceDate: April 2023, issue 3, review Sept 2026 (six month extension approved)

scenario: An urgent Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) authorisation is running out and the standard authorisation has not yet been dealt with.
question: What does the trust DoLS policy say about extending it?
options: The Managing Authority may ask the Supervisory Body to extend it by a maximum of a further 7 days, and the request must be made before the current authorisation expires
It can be extended once by 28 days by the ward manager
It rolls over automatically until the Supervisory Body responds
It can be extended for a further 14 days by the responsible clinician
rationale: The policy allows a request to the Supervisory Body to extend an urgent authorisation for a maximum of a further 7 days, in exceptional circumstances, and states the request must come before the expiry of the present urgent authorisation.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Deprivation of Liberty (DoLS) Policy and Procedures
sourceDate: April 2023, issue 3, review Sept 2026 (six month extension approved)

question: In the standard Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) form set listed in the trust policy, which form is used by the Managing Authority to request a standard or an urgent authorisation, and to extend an urgent authorisation?
options: Form 2
Form 1
Form 5
Form 10
rationale: The policy lists Form 1 for requesting a standard or urgent authorisation, including where the Managing Authority gives itself an urgent authorisation, and notes it can also be used to extend the urgent authorisation. Form 2 is a further standard authorisation, Form 5 is the Supervisory Body granting authorisation, and Form 10 covers suspension or review.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Deprivation of Liberty (DoLS) Policy and Procedures
sourceDate: April 2023, issue 3, review Sept 2026 (six month extension approved)

scenario: A patient on a Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) authorisation is being transferred to another trust unit.
question: What does the trust DoLS policy say happens to the existing authorisation?
options: It transfers with the patient for the remainder of its period
It stays valid for 7 days after the move to allow a new application
It stays valid provided the Supervisory Body is the same local authority
It ceases to be valid, and the accepting hospital or care home must apply for its own authorisation
rationale: The policy states that on transfer to another hospital, unit or care home the authorisation ceases to be valid, and those coordinating the transfer must advise the accepting service that it needs to apply to continue depriving the person of their liberty.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Deprivation of Liberty (DoLS) Policy and Procedures
sourceDate: April 2023, issue 3, review Sept 2026 (six month extension approved)

question: Under the trust Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) policy, whose listed responsibility is it to notify the Care Quality Commission (CQC) of new DoLS authorisations?
options: The Supervisory Body (the local authority)
The Mental Health Act (MHA) office
The responsible clinician
The ward staff
rationale: Notifying the CQC of new authorisations is listed in the policy under Ward Staff responsibilities, alongside uploading completed forms to the electronic patient record, notifying the Mental Health Act office, and keeping a record of DoLS patients and expiry dates.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Deprivation of Liberty (DoLS) Policy and Procedures
sourceDate: April 2023, issue 3, review Sept 2026 (six month extension approved)

scenario: The ward has contacted the local authority for a Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) assessment and days are passing with no assessor allocated.
question: Which role does the trust DoLS policy say records the request and chases the local authority?
options: The Mental Capacity Act (MCA) / Mental Health Act (MHA) Team Leader
The ward manager
The on call manager
The Assistant Director of Safeguarding Adults
rationale: The policy says the MCA/MHA team leader is alerted when ward staff contact the local authority, records the request, and if there are delays in a DoLS assessor coming to the ward will contact the local authority on a regular basis to ensure the assessment is completed.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Deprivation of Liberty (DoLS) Policy and Procedures
sourceDate: April 2023, issue 3, review Sept 2026 (six month extension approved)

question: In the trust Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) policy, who is the Managing Authority and who is the Supervisory Body?
options: The Managing Authority is the Care Quality Commission (CQC) and the Supervisory Body is the Trust
The Managing Authority is the responsible clinician and the Supervisory Body is the Mental Health Act (MHA) office
The Managing Authority is the local authority and the Supervisory Body is the Court of Protection
The Managing Authority is the Trust, via the Ward Manager, and the Supervisory Body is the relevant local authority
rationale: The definitions section of the policy states that for the purposes of the policy the Managing Authority means the Trust, via the Ward Manager, and the Supervisory Body is the relevant local authority for the area (Derby City Council or Derbyshire County Council).
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Deprivation of Liberty (DoLS) Policy and Procedures
sourceDate: April 2023, issue 3, review Sept 2026 (six month extension approved)

question: According to the trust Consent to Examination and Treatment policy, which is the only treatment given in this Trust where the consent forms referred to in that policy must be used?
options: Rapid Tranquillisation (RT)
Depot antipsychotic medication
Clozapine initiation
Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT)
rationale: The policy states that ECT is the only treatment within the Trust where its consent forms must be used, while reminding staff that separate statutory Mental Health Act forms such as T2, T3 and CTO11 apply where relevant.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Consent to Examination and Treatment Policy and Procedure

question: Appendix A of the trust Consent to Examination and Treatment policy lists the consent forms in use. Which numbered form is recorded as no longer in use in this organisation?
options: Form 1
Form 2
Form 3
Form 4
rationale: The policy lists three versions in use, Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) consent forms 1, 2 and 4, and states Form 3 is no longer in use in this organisation. All are held with the Approved Forms on the trust intranet.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Consent to Examination and Treatment Policy and Procedure

scenario: A patient whose first language is not English needs a detailed treatment discussion and you want a face to face interpreter.
question: What does the trust Consent to Examination and Treatment policy say about arranging this?
options: Onsite interpreters are available where 24 hours notice of need is given, and telephone translation is available in the meantime
Onsite interpreters must be booked at least one week ahead
A family member should interpret wherever one is available
Interpreters can only be booked by the Mental Health Act (MHA) office
rationale: The policy states the Trust has full access to telephone translation services and onsite interpreters where 24 hours notice of need is required. It also states that using a relative or friend as interpreter is not good practice and should only happen in exceptional circumstances.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Consent to Examination and Treatment Policy and Procedure

scenario: It is a Sunday night and a complex consent and capacity dispute on the ward needs legal advice before morning.
question: Under the arrangements set out in the trust Consent to Examination and Treatment policy, how is out of hours legal advice obtained?
options: Any registered nurse may instruct the Trust's solicitors directly
Through the second on call Executive Director, who can access external legal providers
By emailing the Legal Services Manager and waiting for the next working day
Through the Care Quality Commission (CQC) out of hours line
rationale: Appendix C of the policy, taken from the Accessing Legal Advice Policy, states the Trust has access to out of hours legal advice via external legal providers and that advice from those firms can be sought via the second on call Executive Director. In hours, staff go via their line manager to the Legal Services Manager and should not instruct solicitors directly.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Consent to Examination and Treatment Policy and Procedure

scenario: An adult lacks capacity to consent to admission and treatment, and is clearly objecting to both.
question: According to the trust Consent to Examination and Treatment policy, which legal framework is available?
options: A Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) authorisation
A Court of Protection order
Formal admission under the Mental Health Act 1983 only
A best interests decision under the Mental Capacity Act (MCA) alone
rationale: The policy states that where an adult lacks capacity and objects to admission and treatment, the only legal framework available is formal admission under the Mental Health Act 1983, and that for the avoidance of doubt neither a Court of Protection order nor DoLS are available. Where the patient lacks capacity and does not object, all three may be available.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Consent to Examination and Treatment Policy and Procedure

question: Under the monitoring section of the trust Consent to Examination and Treatment policy, who coordinates the audit of the consent process and where do the results go?
options: The ward manager, reporting to the Mental Health Act (MHA) Committee
The Care Quality Commission (CQC), with results presented to the Trust
The Legal Services Manager, with results presented to the Board
The Audit Manager, with results presented to the Quality Governance Committee
rationale: The policy states the consent audit is coordinated by the Audit Manager and the results are presented to the Quality Governance Committee, with incidents, complaints and claims reported through the Risk Management Committee and learning shared in the Trust Lessons Learned newsletter.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Consent to Examination and Treatment Policy and Procedure

scenario: A colleague asks you to obtain consent for a procedure they are about to carry out.
question: Under the trust Consent to Examination and Treatment policy, who is ultimately responsible for ensuring the patient is genuinely consenting?
options: The health professional carrying out the procedure
The nurse in charge of the shift
The person who signs the consent form as witness
The responsible clinician for the ward
rationale: The policy states the health professional carrying out the procedure is ultimately responsible for ensuring the patient is genuinely consenting, and that it is they who will be held responsible in law if this is challenged later. It also says professionals must be confident that any colleague they ask to seek consent is competent to do so.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Consent to Examination and Treatment Policy and Procedure

scenario: A relative arrives on the ward saying they hold Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) for the patient and want to make decisions about care.
question: What does the trust Advance Decisions, Advance Statements and Lasting Power of Attorney policy require staff to do?
options: Accept the relative's word and record it in the notes
Refer them straight to the Court of Protection
View a copy of the document and establish whether it is registered with the Office of the Public Guardian, because an unregistered LPA is ineffective
Ask the responsible clinician to decide whether to involve them
rationale: The policy says patients should routinely be asked if they have an LPA, that it must be recorded on the health record and trust electronic record with details of its nature, and that staff should view a copy and know whether it is registered with the Office of the Public Guardian. An unregistered LPA is ineffective, and only a personal welfare attorney can be a decision maker on welfare matters.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Advance Decisions to Refuse Medical Treatment, Advance Statements and Lasting Power of Attorney Policy

scenario: There is genuine doubt about whether a claimed Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) actually exists.
question: Which form does the trust policy say is used to request that information from the Office of the Public Guardian (OPG)?
options: Form OPG 100
Form LPA 114
Form COP 1
Form T3
rationale: The policy states that if there are doubts regarding the existence of an LPA, form OPG 100 is used to request this information from the Office of the Public Guardian.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Advance Decisions to Refuse Medical Treatment, Advance Statements and Lasting Power of Attorney Policy

scenario: A member of staff says they cannot in conscience follow a patient's valid advance decision refusing life sustaining treatment.
question: What does the trust policy say should happen?
options: They must follow it regardless of their beliefs
They should raise it with their manager, and the patient's care must be transferred quickly to a professional who has no objection
The advance decision should be referred to the Court of Protection to be overturned
The responsible clinician should decide whether the advance decision still stands
rationale: The policy says a member of staff who disagrees in principle must bring this to their manager's attention. They do not have to act against their beliefs, but the patient's care must not be affected and so must be quickly transferred to another professional who has no objection to following the advance decision.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Advance Decisions to Refuse Medical Treatment, Advance Statements and Lasting Power of Attorney Policy

question: The trust policy on advance decisions points to the trust systems that alert staff that an advance decision or advance statement exists. Which standard of the Minimum Standards for Health Records deals with alerts?
options: Standard 2
Standard 5
Standard 8
Standard 11
rationale: The policy states that Standard 8 of the Minimum Standards for Health Records deals with alerts, requiring an Administrative Alert in the relevant record, and that for electronic records a Clinical Alert can be created showing an advance decision or advance statement has been made.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Advance Decisions to Refuse Medical Treatment, Advance Statements and Lasting Power of Attorney Policy

question: The trust policy describes two categories of person who can give a Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) certificate. What defines a Category A certificate provider?
options: A relative of the donor who lives at the same address
A person chosen by the donor who has known them for at least 2 years
Any registered health professional involved in the donor's care
A person appointed by the Court of Protection
rationale: The policy sets out that Category A is a person chosen by the donor who has known the person for at least 2 years, while Category B is someone with relevant professional skills. Family members of the donor, the attorney, and care home staff are disqualified from giving a certificate.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Advance Decisions to Refuse Medical Treatment, Advance Statements and Lasting Power of Attorney Policy

scenario: A patient is admitted with a ReSPECT form in their notes.
question: What does the trust policy say about how ReSPECT relates to an Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment (ADRT)?
options: ReSPECT replaces any ADRT the patient has made
ReSPECT only applies to patients on end of life care pathways, so an ADRT overrides it
ReSPECT and an ADRT cannot both be held for the same patient
ReSPECT replaced the Do Not Attempt Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (DNACPR) form, and does not replace an ADRT but should signpost staff to it and summarise its content
rationale: The policy states that ReSPECT replaced the DNACPR documentation, and that the ReSPECT form does not replace an ADRT but should signpost clinical staff to the existence of an ADRT and provide a summary of its content, referring staff to the ReSPECT policy.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Advance Decisions to Refuse Medical Treatment, Advance Statements and Lasting Power of Attorney Policy

question: The trust Mental Capacity Policy states that its approach to assessing capacity differs from the Mental Capacity Act (MCA) Code of Practice. What is the trust's stated approach?
options: Establish the impairment or disturbance of mind or brain first, and only then apply the four part functional test
Apply the four part functional test first, and only if the person cannot do one of those four things consider whether that is because of an impairment or disturbance of mind or brain
Assess capacity only where a doctor has requested it
Assess capacity globally rather than decision by decision
rationale: The policy sets out the functional test (understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate) first, and only where the person cannot do one of those does the clinician go on to consider impairment or disturbance and whether the inability is because of it. The policy states this is consistent with case law, which overrides the Code.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Mental Capacity Policy (Overarching)

scenario: A patient's behaviour has changed markedly with no obvious explanation, and they are making a decision that carries real risk. A colleague says capacity is presumed so nothing needs recording.
question: What does the trust Mental Capacity Policy say?
options: The presumption of capacity means no record is needed unless an assessment is done
Capacity should only be assessed if the patient asks for one
Clinicians must be prepared to explain why they decided not to carry out a capacity assessment, and should not record that capacity is presumed where there is legitimate reason to doubt it
A full assessment is required for every patient on the ward every week
rationale: The policy states that clinicians must be prepared to explain why they decided not to carry out a capacity assessment, and should not record that capacity is presumed where there is legitimate reason to doubt it, such as an unexplained change in presentation or behaviour, especially where the decision may cause harm.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Mental Capacity Policy (Overarching)

scenario: On admission you assess a patient's capacity to consent to sharing their clinical information with family and carers, and they have capacity.
question: What does Appendix 2 of the trust Mental Capacity Policy say you do next?
options: Assist the patient to complete the Advance Statement form in the trust Sharing Information with Family and Carers booklet, then scan the form onto SystmOne and give a copy of the form and booklet to the patient and carers
Record their verbal agreement in the daily notes and take no further action
Complete a Best Interest form and inform the carers of the outcome
Ask the carers to sign an information sharing agreement
rationale: Appendix 2 sets out that where the patient has capacity, staff assist them to complete the Advance Statement form in the trust Sharing Information with Family and Carers booklet, documenting their wishes on sharing if capacity is later lost, then scan the form onto SystmOne and give a copy of the form and booklet to the patient and carers.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Mental Capacity Policy (Overarching)

scenario: A best interests decision about serious medical treatment is contentious and cannot be resolved by the team.
question: What does the trust Mental Capacity Policy say about going to court?
options: The patient's family must apply to the Court of Protection themselves
For serious or major medical treatment decisions the Trust will usually make the application, and this should be discussed with the Legal Department
The ward manager applies to the Court of Protection using the DoLS forms
Applications are always made by the local authority as Supervisory Body
rationale: The policy states that for cases about serious or major decisions concerning medical treatment the Trust will usually make an application to the Court, that controversial and complex best interests decisions should be discussed with the Legal Department, and that where social care staff are concerned about a welfare decision the relevant local authority should make the application.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - Mental Capacity Policy (Overarching)

scenario: A patient lacking capacity needs help with washing, dressing, meals and getting to a hospital appointment.
question: According to the trust Capacity Manual on best interests, how is this normally handled?
options: A formal Best Interest Meeting must be held before any personal care is given
It is recorded by ticking the routine care best interests box on the capacity to consent record, which does not require a formal Best Interest Meeting
It requires an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate (IMCA) referral in every case
It requires written agreement from the next of kin
rationale: The manual states that for routine care, an acknowledgement that it is being provided in the patient's best interests can be recorded by ticking the relevant box in the capacity to consent record, and that this does not require a formal Best Interest Meeting. It lists washing, dressing, food, fluids, essential medication, mobility, ward activities and hospital appointments as examples of routine care.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - DHCFT Capacity Manual: Best Interests
reviewFlag: predates the move from PARIS to SystmOne - check current form names before use

scenario: The team is considering covert medication for a patient who lacks capacity.
question: What does the trust Capacity Manual on best interests indicate about this type of decision?
options: It can be treated as routine care and simply recorded on the capacity to consent form
It is a medical decision for the doctor alone and needs no wider discussion
It always requires an application to the Court of Protection
It is the kind of decision, involving a range of professionals in a specific intervention, for which a formal Best Interest Meeting should be held
rationale: The manual gives covert medication as an example of a decision involving a range of professionals in a specific intervention, which sits in its list of circumstances where a formal Best Interest Meeting should be held, along with complex, contentious or risk laden decisions, major life decisions and decisions with legal consequences.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - DHCFT Capacity Manual: Best Interests
reviewFlag: predates the move from PARIS to SystmOne - check current form names before use

scenario: A formal Best Interest Meeting is arranged but the patient's social worker and one carer cannot attend.
question: What does the trust Capacity Manual on best interests say should happen?
options: The meeting should be postponed until everyone invited can attend
Only professionals in attendance may contribute to the decision
Non attendance is taken as agreement with the decision reached
Their opinions should be sought and recorded beforehand, raised at the meeting on their behalf, and they should be informed of the outcome afterwards
rationale: The manual says all relevant parties should be invited, including relevant professionals, carers and where appropriate the patient's Independent Mental Capacity Advocate (IMCA), and that where some cannot attend you seek and record their opinions beforehand, raise these during the meeting on their behalf, and inform them of the outcome afterwards.
source: Derbyshire Healthcare - DHCFT Capacity Manual: Best Interests
